explanations.explanation: Yes, the Herodians. The text says the Pharisees sent their disciples to Him "…along with the Herodians." So the question comes from that group, not from the Pharisees themselves. Sending a whole delegation to ask one question is a plan with a lot of moving parts.
Not the Samaritans. Matthew 22:16 says the Pharisees sent their disciples to Him "…along with the Herodians." The Samaritans aren't named in that verse. The Herodians are the answer here, friend.

Not the Levites. The text says the Pharisees sent their disciples "…along with the Herodians." The Levites aren't named in this verse. Look at who goes with the disciples, and you'll find the Herodians.

It's actually the opposite. They say, "…You pay no attention to external appearance." In other words, they say Jesus doesn't judge by how someone looks. They're stacking the compliments pretty high at this point. I'd be checking my pockets by now.

Right, because the text says the opposite. They tell Jesus, "You seek favor from no one, because You pay no attention to external appearance." That's another compliment on the pile. They keep stacking them higher and higher, like cookies on one plate.

Yes, taxes. They ask, "Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?" The text says the Pharisees conspired to trap Jesus in His words (Matthew 22:15). So this yes-or-no question comes straight out of that plan. Keep that in mind as the story goes on, baker.
That's not the word they use. They ask, "Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?" The word in the verse is taxes. It's a close guess, but tithes isn't what they say.
Not wages, though I'd love a question about my wages sometime. They ask, "Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?" The word is taxes. Wages never come up in their question.

That's it. Jesus says, "You hypocrites, why are you testing Me?" The text tells us He knew their evil intent. All those sweet words were sitting on top of something else. And He names it right away, with no wind-up.
Jesus doesn't call them thieves here. He says, "You hypocrites, why are you testing Me?" The text says He knew their evil intent. They came with nice words, and He answers what was really going on.

Not strangers. Jesus says, "You hypocrites, why are you testing Me?" The text says He knew their evil intent. They came in like old friends with all those compliments, but Jesus wasn't fooled for a second.

Yes, the same men who came to test Him. Jesus says, "Show Me the coin used for the tax." and the text says, "…they brought Him a denarius." So the men testing Him are the ones who bring the coin. I think it's funny that their test brings its own coin, but that's just me.

Simon Peter, one of Jesus' twelve disciples (Matthew 10:2), isn't named in this passage. The text says "…they brought Him a denarius." That "they" is the ones who came to Him with the question in verse 16. Good guess on a name you know, though.

Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve disciples (Matthew 10:4), isn't in this passage. After Jesus asks for the coin, the text says "…they brought Him a denarius." That "they" is the group who came to test Him. They're the ones holding the coin.

Caesar's! Jesus asks whose image and inscription are on the coin, and they answer, “Caesar’s.” Now the men who came with all the questions are the ones answering, and they're the ones who brought Him the coin (Matthew 22:19). That's like walking into a meeting to grill somebody and ending up presenting the slides. Their own answer sets up what Jesus says next.

Herod isn't the name they give. Asked whose image and inscription are on the coin, they answer, "Caesar’s." It's the same Caesar from the tax question. Then Jesus talks about Caesar and God, not Herod.

Pilate, the Roman governor (Matthew 27:2), isn't named here. When Jesus asks whose image and inscription are on the coin, they answer, "Caesar's." That's the same Caesar they asked about from the start. One name, one coin, and no governor in sight.

Jesus doesn't say that. The text says, "Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s." So He doesn't tell them to refuse the tax. Look at how He answers, baker. The coin does the talking.

Right. What Jesus actually says is, "Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s." He never tells them not to pay. He answers the question with the coin they brought Him, and with one line about Caesar and God.
Yes. The text says, "…when they heard this, they were amazed." Then they left Him and went away. They came to trap Him in His words, and they walked away amazed instead. I'd be amazed too, baker.

Nope, that's False, friend. The text says, “…when they heard this, they were amazed.” Then they left Him and went away. They showed up with a trap all planned, like somebody carrying a full presentation into a meeting and leaving without ever opening the laptop. I bet that walk away was a quiet one.
